title: Merrick Neck Lands and Bay Villages
summary: Merrick histories describe villages on south shore necks of land along the Great South Bay, tying Merrick and nearby Freeport-area community life to bays, meadows, creeks, fishing, shellfishing, travel, and archaeological memory.
address_label: South shore neck lands, Merrick-Bellmore-Freeport area
ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a south shore community and bay landscape.
why_this_matters: The Merrick neck lands show how Native community life was organized around water, meadow, and bay access. A visitor looking south from Merrick or Bellmore is seeing a landscape that supported fishing, shellfishing, travel, planting, and kinship long before suburban roads and parcels.
introduction_content:
The Merricks are described as having villages on several necks of land along the Great South Bay. Those neck lands connected uplands, salt meadows, tidal creeks, shellfish beds, and bay travel routes in the broader Merrick, Freeport, Baldwin, and Bellmore south shore landscape.

This neck-land landscape should be understood as Native community geography rather than a single village address.
preservation_content: This marker gives a broad orientation to the neck-land and bay-village landscape, including places connected to village life, archaeology, and private shoreline areas.
artifacts_content: Local-history and archaeology sources describe extensive shell deposits and other material traces in the south shore creek-and-meadow landscape. Those traces speak to fishing, shellfishing, travel, and long relationships with the bay, while archaeological places remain vulnerable to disturbance, collecting, trespass, and souvenir hunting. [1. The Illustrated Story of Baldwin Long Island, N.Y.; Baldwin: Our Heritage (1976); James Truex, ed., The Second Coastal Archaeological Reader: 1900 to the Present.]
vandalism_content: Nineteenth- and twentieth-century accounts indicate that some shell deposits in the wider area were removed or repurposed, including for fertilizer. That history is part of the site's meaning: cultural evidence was often damaged before it could be protected, documented with community guidance, or understood as Indigenous heritage. [1. The Illustrated Story of Baldwin Long Island, N.Y.; Baldwin: Our Heritage (1976); James Truex, ed., The Second Coastal Archaeological Reader: 1900 to the Present.]
